observations: Both GPUs retained exact pixel equality for culled/unculled and profiled/unprofiled captures. The offscreen caster still shadows the receiver; hiding/falling it clears that shadow.
The constructed 245-object fixture reduced camera submissions from 245 to 4 and shadow submissions from 1470 to 8 on both GPUs.
Both 371-tick continuous replays matched independent headless state and unculled final capture. Each recorded 372 completed GPU timestamp samples with zero dropped samples.
The NVIDIA fixture image was visually inspected: a visible receiver retains the large shadow from an offscreen caster.

Existing shadow tests passed all cascades/blend boundaries, six point faces/seam, all supported resolutions, final array layer, indexed/hidden/moving casters and smooth-normal receiver-plane checks under default culling.
limits: Draw reductions describe a deliberately offscreen-heavy correctness fixture, not a representative game speedup.
Initial culling captures overlapped a CPU runtime build. Their tiny two-frame timings are diagnostics, not a controlled performance benchmark.
Timestamp intervals use one graphics queue, valid-bit masking and actual device periods. GPU stages overlap; the four boundaries are approximate and instrumentation has overhead.
The renderer still serializes FIFO submissions with a per-frame GPU wait. Capture includes readback; timing excludes full game simulation, presentation completion and file encoding.
No hierarchical scene index, occlusion culling, instanced batching, resource streaming, shadow caching or production render graph is supplied by this change.
Evidence covers two GPUs in one laptop on native Windows through WSL interop. Intel, native Linux hardware, other machines, MSVC builds and consoles remain unqualified.
NVRHI validation reported no errors; full Khronos Vulkan validation and physical human-input qualification remain outstanding.
